opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think it was one of the better decisions I made, even though at the time it wasn't some grand strategic plan. Coming from China, I didn't know much about the American college landscape. A liberal arts college felt like a place where I could explore before committing to one narrow path.

What I appreciate most now is the breadth. I wasn't only taking computer science and math. I was also reading philosophy, writing a lot, and sitting in small seminars where you couldn't hide in the back row. You had to speak up and defend your ideas. That shaped how I think and communicate, and in research that turns out to matter a lot. Half of the job is figuring out which questions are worth asking and then explaining why they matter to other people.

The small size also meant professors actually knew you. I could walk into a faculty member's office and talk about an idea, or ask to get involved in a project, and they would take me seriously as an undergrad. That kind of mentorship is harder to get at a big research university, where you might be one of hundreds of students in a lecture.

Of course, there were trade-offs. A small college doesn't have the huge labs, the cutting-edge robotics facilities, or as many PhD students to learn from. When I moved on to more research-heavy environments, I had some catching up to do on the technical side, and I had to be quite proactive in seeking out research opportunities.

But overall, I think the foundation it gave me, curiosity across fields, learning how to learn, and feeling comfortable with open-ended problems, has been really valuable, especially in a field like robotics and AI, where so many of the interesting questions sit at the boundaries between disciplines. So I don't regret it at all. If anything, I'd encourage students not to dismiss liberal arts colleges just because they're less well known for engineering.

r001.rationale: He says the college let him explore before committing to a narrow path.

r002.rationale: He says professors knew him, took him seriously as an undergraduate, and he could ask them to involve him in a project, linking that mentorship to research opportunities.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I look back on it as one of the best accidents of my life. I didn't go to Dickinson with some grand plan. I ended up there partly because the application process and the campus just felt right, and partly because I didn't really know what I wanted to do yet. And that turned out to be exactly the point.

At a liberal arts college you're kind of forced to be a generalist for a while. I took philosophy, I took writing-heavy courses, I took things that had nothing to do with computer science. At the time I sometimes wondered if I was falling behind friends at big engineering schools who were already deep into systems courses as freshmen. But what I got instead was a lot of practice thinking about questions rather than just answering them. In research, and especially in robotics and AI, the hard part is usually not implementing the thing. It's figuring out what the right problem is, why it matters, and how to communicate it. Those were muscles I built at Dickinson without realizing it.

The other thing was access. It's a small place, so I could actually sit in a professor's office and talk through ideas, and I got to do real research as an undergrad, which is not a given at a bigger school where there are hundreds of students competing for a few lab spots. That early exposure is what pushed me toward a PhD.

There were trade-offs, of course. The CS department was small, so I had to be proactive, do a lot of self-study, and seek out opportunities off campus. But that also taught me to be resourceful. So if I'm honest, I wouldn't change it. It made me a better researcher and probably a more interesting person than I would have been otherwise.

r001.rationale: He describes being able to explore broadly through philosophy, writing, and other subjects while he was still figuring out his direction, and says this benefited his development.

r002.rationale: He says the small college let him talk through ideas with professors and get undergraduate research experience, which pushed him toward a PhD.
